title: Detect Social Engineering
summary: This detection strategy covers social engineering activity: email, messaging and voice contact that persuades a person to take an action rather than exploiting a technical flaw. It covers technique T1684 and matters because the human channel bypasses controls entirely, and because the first warning is often a message that looks almost legitimate. The telemetry that makes it possible is mail gateway metadata and headers, sender and domain reputation, first contact relationships between sender and recipient, collaboration platform message events, and endpoint process creation when a document or link is followed. In practice the strategy fails because the malicious content is designed to look normal, and because the same pattern is produced by legitimate suppliers, recruiters and bulk mail. The workable approach scores several weak signals together, such as a new sender, a lookalike domain, urgency wording in the subject and an unusual request, and then confirms with human reporting.

beginner.definition: Social engineering means tricking a person into doing something, such as opening a file or paying an invoice. This detection looks for messages and contact patterns that try to do that. It catches the attempt, not a software bug.
beginner.whyItMatters: Firewalls and antivirus tools do not stop a polite or frightening message. The attacker only needs one person to trust it. These messages often arrive first, before any tool is touched. If you spot the pattern early, you can warn people and block the sender before anyone acts.
howItWorks: You collect mail gateway data. This includes the sender, the reply address and the subject.
You check the sender's domain and its age, and whether it is close to a domain you trust.
You check whether this sender has written to this person before. A first contact is a signal.
You look at the message body for pressure words or for a payment or password request.
You watch endpoints for the moment a user opens an attachment or follows a link.
You combine these signals and send the highest scoring messages for human review.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital reception desk. A stranger in a white coat smiles and says he is the new doctor. Nobody checked the badge. The coat and the confidence were the whole trick. Social engineering works like that: a friendly, urgent story is used instead of a forced door.
takeaways: Social engineering attacks people, so your people are also your sensors.
A first contact between sender and recipient is one of the strongest signals you have.
Lookalike domains and pressure wording together beat either signal alone.

objectives: Define social engineering and distinguish it from technical exploitation of a software weakness
Identify the mail and collaboration metadata fields that indicate a first contact or a lookalike sender domain
Compare a sender domain against protected brand names using edit distance rather than exact matching
Correlate a suspicious message with the endpoint event that followed it, such as attachment execution or link redirection
Describe how user reports and mailbox rule indicators feed a social engineering detection programme
Set escalation criteria for invoice fraud, credential requests and executive impersonation
dataSources: Mail gateway message metadata including envelope sender, header from address, reply to address, subject and receiving IP address
Domain registration age and Domain Name System (DNS) records for the sending domain, including SPF, DKIM and DMARC results
Mailbox audit records of inbox rule creation or forwarding rule changes made shortly after message delivery
Collaboration platform message and file share audit events naming the external sender and the recipient channel
Windows Security event 4688 process creation or Sysmon event 1 showing a document reader or browser launched as the parent of a script interpreter
logic: The pattern is an unsolicited contact that asks for a trust based action from someone who has no prior relationship with the sender. You correlate the sending domain, its registration age and authentication results with the mailbox history between that sender and the recipient, and with the endpoint events that occur within minutes of message delivery. The malicious case is a first time sender using a domain that is textually close to a trusted brand, failing authentication checks, asking for a payment change or credentials, followed by a file execution or a credential prompt on the recipient host. The benign case is a new but correctly authenticated supplier domain, with consistent message history building after the first contact and no endpoint follow through. Time proximity between the message and the endpoint event is what lifts this from a mail triage queue into an incident.
pseudoQuery:
# title: First Contact Sender With Lookalike Domain and Urgent Payment Request
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: email
# detection:
#   selection:
#     first_contact: true
#     domain_age_days: < 90
#     subject|contains:
#       - 'urgent'
#       - 'invoice'
#       - 'payment'
#       - 'password'
#     dmarc_result: fail
#   condition: selection
# level: medium
falsePositives: Recruiters and candidates writing from a newly registered personal or agency domain for the first time
New suppliers sending their first invoice with a legitimate but recently created trading domain
Automated notification services that send from a subdomain not previously seen and use urgent sounding wording
Conference and event organisers using a short lived registration domain for speaker or travel communication
Internal marketing campaigns that send from an external bulk mail platform and land outside established sender history
tuningNotes: Filter out correctly authenticated bulk senders and any domain that appears in your supplier master list, but keep alerting on lookalike domains even when they authenticate, because attackers do register real domains. Scope the highest severity tier to finance, human resources and executive assistants, where invoice and payroll fraud have the largest impact. Baseline your organisation's normal first contact rate so the alert threshold follows real volume. Requiring several signals at once removes noise but also misses a well written single technique message, so keep a separate low severity detection driven purely by user reports to catch what the scoring model misses.
